James.1: Having enough time for my personal and home life is of utmost importance to me, as I've seen too many blokes in trades burn out from long hours and miss out on family time, and I value balance over just chasing money.
James.2: Having a boss I can respect is very important because it makes the workday smoother and motivates me to do my best work without constant friction. In my experience as a tradie, a good boss who knows their stuff and treats you fair makes all the difference.
James.3: Getting recognition for good performance is very important to me because it motivates me to keep doing my best work and shows that my efforts are valued by the team or boss. In my experience as a tradie, a pat on the back or a shout-out makes the hard yards worthwhile.
James.4: As a bloke who's been in trades for years, having a steady job without the worry of sudden layoffs is very important to me, especially with a family to support and bills to pay. It gives peace of mind to focus on the work without constant job-hunting stress.
James.5: Working with pleasant people makes the job much more enjoyable and reduces stress, which is very important to me after dealing with difficult characters in trades work.
James.6: Work has to be interesting or it's just a grind that kills your soul day after day; life's too short to hate what you do for 40 hours a week.
James.7: As a technician, I value being consulted on work decisions because my hands-on experience helps make better calls, but it's not the top priority if the boss knows their stuff. It keeps things running smoothly without me needing to run the show.
James.8: Very important because as a bloke who's worked hard in trades across Australia, I'd want my ideal job to let me settle in a nice spot like near the coast or a good regional town with decent weather and lifestyle, not stuck in some remote shithole site. It'd make the daily grind way more bearable after years of FIFO bullshit.
James.9: It's moderately important to have a job that my family and friends respect, as I value their opinions from my working-class background, but it wouldn't stop me from doing something I enjoy if they didn't fully get it.
James.10: At my age and with my experience as a tradie, chances for promotion are moderately important as they offer some career growth, but I'm more focused on job security, good pay, and work-life balance than climbing the ladder.
James.12: As a bloke who's worked hard in trades all my life, I value getting what I need to enjoy life, like a cold beer after work or a good ute, but I don't see much point in denying myself simple pleasures just for the sake of moderation. Too many desires? Nah, life's too short not to chase a bit of what makes you happy.
James.13: Doing a service to a friend is of utmost importance to me because mateship is core to Aussie values and I've always believed in helping out your mates without expecting anything back, as it's built lifelong loyalty in my life.
James.14: Very important - I've always lived by the principle of not wasting money, especially after years in trades where every dollar counts towards tools and family needs.

James.16: Life as a tradie in Australia has its ups and downs with work and family, but I usually find reasons to be happy most days.
James.17: Sometimes life throws curveballs like work commitments or family needs that get in the way, but I usually find a way to make things happen.
James.18: I'm in good health overall, stay active with my trade work and keep fit enough to handle the physical demands without major issues. No serious complaints, just the usual aches from years on the tools.
James.19: I'm very proud to be Australian because we've got a fair go for everyone, stunning natural beauty from the Outback to the beaches, and a resilient spirit shaped by our history of mateship and hard work. It's the best country in the world to raise a family and get ahead with your own two hands.
James.20: In my experience as a technician, subordinates usually hold back from contradicting the boss to avoid conflict or risking their job, though it happens sometimes with more confident workers. I've seen it in trade environments where hierarchy is strong.
James.21: Strongly agree because as a technician, I've seen plenty of good managers who don't know every technical detail but guide their teams effectively by knowing when to delegate or seek expert advice. No one can possibly have all the answers, and good management is about leadership and resources, not being an encyclopedia.
James.22: Strongly agree. In my years as a technician, I've seen that sticking at a job persistently, troubleshooting step by step, always gets results no matter how tough it is. Giving up too early never works.
